item.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory.
item.description:
eLife
Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity-brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay-in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal-neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

item.title: Balance dısorders and structural and connectıvıty changes in the cerebellum in bıpolar dısorder: A dıffusıon tensor imagıng study.
item.description:
The neuroradiology journal
The aim of this study was to evaluate balance performance in individuals with bipolar disorder (BD) and to examine changes in white matter connections associated with cerebellar structures using cranial magnetic resonance (MR) imaging.The study included 30 BD patients and 25 healthy controls with available cranial MR images. Balance performance was assessed, and tractography analyses examined the pathways of the superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP), middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP), inferior cerebellar peduncle (ICP), medial lemniscus (LM), and vermis bilaterally. In addition, volumetric measurements of the cerebellum and its subregions were performed.Balance performance was significantly lower in individuals with BD compared to the control group (p < .05). In tractography analyses, a significant decrease in FA values was observed only in the SCP compared to the control group (p = .029). Volumetric analyses revealed a significant decrease in total cerebellar volume in the BB group (p < .05).These findings suggest that individuals with BB may exhibit impaired balance performance, particularly at the SCP level, along with reduced cerebellar volume and limited microstructural changes. While these results suggest a potential role for the cerebellum in the pathophysiology and balance-related mechanisms of BD, they need to be confirmed with a larger sample and longitudinal studies.

item.title: Frontal Low-Frequency Electroencephalographic Coherence in Bipolar Disorder: A Covariate-Controlled Secondary Analysis of a Public Resting-State EEG Feature Dataset.
item.description:
Clinical EEG and neuroscience
ObjectiveTo test whether bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with predefined frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp electroencephalography (EEG) coherence differences relative to healthy controls (HC), depressive disorder (DD), and schizophrenia (SZ) in a covariate-controlled reanalysis of a public resting-state EEG feature dataset.MethodsThe covariate-complete sample included 472 participants (93 HC, 66 BD, 196 DD, and 117 SZ). Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for age, sex, education, and intelligence quotient (IQ). Primary outcomes were predefined frontal/frontopolar delta, theta, and combined delta-theta coherence means. Electrode-pair, regional, all-frequency, distributional, global-reference, frontopolar, and age sensitivity analyses assessed robustness.ResultsBD had higher adjusted coherence than all comparison groups across the three primary measures (partial η2 = .037-.040); Holm-adjusted BD-HC, BD-DD, and BD-SZ contrasts were significant for each measure. Features surviving false discovery rate correction were concentrated in the delta and theta bands. Findings were robust to distributional, outlier, and global-coherence analyses, but effects were strongest in frontopolar pairs and attenuated as anterior electrodes were excluded.ConclusionsBD showed higher covariate-adjusted frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp coherence than HC within this dataset. Differences from DD and SZ were smaller and concentrated in frontopolar pairs susceptible to ocular artifacts. Because only scalp-level coherence features were available and participant-level artifact-rejection data were unavailable, the findings do not establish a diagnostic biomarker, diagnostic specificity, or source-level mechanism. Artifact-controlled replication is required.

item.title: Depressive symptoms moderate daily anticipated and momentary emotion dynamics and associate with complex brain network topology: Resting-state EEG and ecological momentary assessment evidence.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
BACKGROUND: The dynamic linkage between anticipated and momentary emotion is a core daily regulatory process, yet the psychopathological and neurophysiological mechanisms disrupting this linkage in depression remain unclear. By bridging macroscopic neural topology with microscopic behavioral dynamics, this study investigated the within-person dynamics of these emotions and their cross-level associations with depressive symptoms and brain network topology. METHODS: Integrating resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA; 3 assessments/day), we recruited 96 young adults. Minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis was applied to characterize baseline brain network topology across multiple frequency bands. Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) was employed to examine within-person dynamics and cross-level statistical moderation. RESULTS: Anticipated emotion prospectively predicted subsequent momentary positive emotion (β = .191) and inversely predicted momentary negative emotion (β = -.125). However, baseline depressive symptoms significantly moderated this prospective affective dynamic: Johnson-Neyman analyses identified empirical transition ranges (PHQ-9 scores 5.7-9.7; mild symptom range) beyond which the prospective emotional link attenuated to non-significance. Furthermore, topological metrics in the theta and delta bands exhibited indirect statistical associations with daily emotional dynamics via their cross-sectional relationship with baseline depressive symptoms. CONCLUSIONS: An attenuated prospective association between positive anticipation and subsequent momentary emotional experience represents a key affective alteration in depressive distress. This daily emotional attenuation co-occurs with elevated depressive distress and is indirectly associated with a centralized topological organization in low-frequency resting-state brain networks. These findings provide novel neurophysiological indicators and highlight the critical window for ecological interventions before symptom severity reaches the moderate range.

item.title: The information architecture of the naturalistic human brain
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
How does the brain orchestrate its central currency, information, for complex adaptive cognition in the real world? Here we provide a comprehensive investigation into the spatiotemporal structure of qualitatively distinct modes of information dynamics in the human brain under ecological conditions. Applying a novel framework for information decomposition to fMRI data from individuals watching full-length feature films, we reveal a multidimensional large-scale information architecture, wherein different schemes for storing, transferring, and transforming representations occupy disjoint topographic and network profiles. Further, this architecture reveals a computational division of labour, with certain regions acting as generalists that support multiple information-processing schemes and others specialising in a few. We show how these interactions reconfigure over time, coalescing into a structured cycle synchronised by sensory input, whose elements are tuned to semantic kinematics. Finally, we replicate these findings in an independent, large-scale dataset. Together, we provide a formal and empirical foundation for understanding the principles that govern distributed computation in the human brain during everyday life.

item.title: Rage bait: a neurofunctional signature of moral outrage elicited by social media
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Moral outrage is ubiquitous online, with powerful emotional and motivational consequences for social life. Combining naturalistic fMRI during exposure to short-form social-media videos depicting moral violations with predictive modeling, we developed a neurofunctional signature of subjective moral outrage (MONS) in discovery/validation (n=80/30) cohorts. MONS predicted experienced outrage and punishment tendencies across cohorts. Positive predictive weights encompassed regions implicated in mentalizing, threat detection and action initiation (precuneus, posterior cingulate, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, cerebellum), whereas negative weights involved valuation and behavioral flexibility systems (amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex). Across 11 datasets (n=478), MONS captured anger and disgust but was dissociable from general negative affect and affective arousal. Notably, MONS did not predict perceived moral wrongness in conventional moral judgment paradigms, suggesting that moral outrage is not reducible to more cognitive moral evaluation. Findings provide a moral outrage neurofunctional model that delineates its relationship to other affective states and distinguishes it from traditional moral judgment.

item.title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, yet how interventions reorganise brain dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression using pre- and post-treatment resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from a double-blind randomised controlled trial ( NCT03429075 ). We compared two whole-brain modelling approaches: conventional signal-space modelling describing interactions between regional brain signals, and vortex-space modelling capturing interactions between evolving patterns of local synchronisation. This represents the first application of vortex-space modelling to a psychiatric disorder. Vortex space was more sensitive than signal space in most analyses, including distinguishing treatment-related brain states, relating baseline connectivity to clinical improvement and predicting response to escitalopram. Our results further revealed distinct patterns of reorganisation following the two interventions. Psilocybin produced widespread increases in vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced network modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable changes. Despite these differences, greater increases in brain turbulence (i.e., spatiotemporal variability in local synchronisation) were associated with greater symptom reduction in both treatments, with a significant post-treatment increase in responders. These findings suggest that psilocybin and escitalopram may reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways and yet share dynamical features associated with clinical improvement. Overall, vortex-space modelling offers a promising framework for characterising brain dynamics in depression and its successful treatment.

item.title: The Dual Nature of Syntactic Node Count: Facilitating and Inhibiting Sentence Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Neurolinguistic research on syntactic processing has used Node Count, the number of syntactic nodes assumed to be built at each word, to investigate how structure-building effort affects brain activity. However, several recent studies cast doubt on the presumed link between Node Count and processing effort; they observe negative correlations between Node Count and reading times. These facilitatory effects raise an alternative hypothesis: rather than reflecting structure-building effort, Node Count may index structure-mediated predictability. To test this hypothesis, we first relate Node Count to an information-theoretic measure of contextual support, the pointwise mutual information (PMI) between a word and its context. We then evaluate the relationship between Node Count and reading times from three large-scale naturalistic English datasets. For these analyses, we derive Node Count under three grammar formalisms (phrase-structure grammar, dependency grammar, and combinatory categorial grammar) and multiple parsing strategies. Variants whose count reflects integrative parsing steps correlate positively with PMI and show a dual behavioral profile: robust facilitation in immediate regions, consistent with structure-mediated predictability, and a delayed slowdown in spillover regions, most consistent with the cost of contextual semantic integration. The facilitatory effect explains reading-time variance beyond GPT-2 surprisal, indicating that Node Count has unique psycholinguistic value as an index of human prediction. These results highlight the role of structural representations in human language processing and underscore the need for a careful interpretation of the observed correlations between Node Count and brain activity in neurolinguistic studies.

item.title: Cerebellum–white-matter proportionality is associated with cognition but not explained by lobular anatomy
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background. A previously identified association between whole-cerebellum and cerebral-white-matter (Cer:WM) allocation and cognitive ability does not establish a lobular mechanism. We tested whether this association in Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) ID1000 was robust to a new cerebellar measurement and explained by regional allocation. Methods. First-run T1-weighted scans from 928 participants were processed outcome-blind with FastSurfer/CerebNet v2.6.0. Before regional measurements were joined to cognition, the primary exposure was fixed as the log ratio of bilateral Crus I, Crus II and VIIb to bilateral lobules I-IV and V. Blinded quality control produced one anatomical exclusion; final analyses used 925 participants and adjusted for age, sex, tissue scale and five-part macroanatomical composition. Results. The newly measured Cer:WM association remained positive (standardized β = 0.101, 95% CI 0.029–0.174, p=.0063; old/new cerebellar totals r=.982). The locked posterior:anterior ratio was null (β = 0.004, 95% CI -0.059-0.067, p=.908); its confidence interval excluded standardized effects of magnitude ≥ 0.067, and a post-hoc equivalence test supported equivalence within ± 0.10 (TOST p=.0014). The regional term attenuated the baseline macro Cer:WM coefficient by only 0.28%. Global lobular-composition and asymmetry tests were null, and regional augmentation was uninformative in cross-validation. Conclusions. The AOMIC Cer:WM association is robust to cerebellar measurement method but is not explained by detectable lobular allocation in healthy young adults. Cerebral white matter and cerebellum showed markedly different intracranial-volume scaling (exponents 0.606 versus 0.372), underscoring allometric and compositional specification as an important benchmark for cerebellar morphometry.

item.title: Diffusion tractography of the olfactory pathway and odor recognition
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Olfactory processing constitutes a unique system where sensory input is directly linked to integrative perceptual processing, providing an optimal model for investigating how perceptual input is transformed into higher-order functions. However, the neural substrates of olfaction remain incompletely understood. Here, we delineated central olfactory pathways using advanced tractography and examined associations between tractography metrics and olfactory functions. We acquired T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted images from 129 healthy participants and assessed olfactory function in 59 individuals using a T&T olfactometer. We defined the primary olfactory cortex and secondary olfactory structures and their connections. White matter query language was used to extract central olfactory pathways from refined whole-brain tractography according to neuroanatomical rules. We analyzed the number of streamlines and the laterality index of these pathways in relation to olfactory detection and recognition thresholds. For the total olfactory fascicle, more streamlines were observed in the left than the right hemisphere, and greater leftward lateralization was significantly associated with lower mean recognition thresholds. In conclusion, we successfully reconstructed central olfactory pathways beyond the primary olfactory cortex and provided evidence supporting the neural basis of higher-order olfactory functions. Leftward lateralization may enhance associative olfactory processing by reducing circuit redundancy and allocating additional neural capacity.

item.title: Correspondence Between Structural and Functional Connectivity Within White Matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract White matter functional networks (WMFNs) derived from resting-state BOLD fluctuations have been identified across multiple datasets, but whether they correspond to coherent anatomical units defined by the underlying axonal architecture remains untested. Here we tested WM structural connectivity-functional connectivity (SC-FC) coupling directly by asking whether regions co-assigned to the same WMFN are preferentially linked by WM tracts. Using resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI from the Human Connectome Project 7T dataset (N = 161), we derived 11 WMFNs per session (after exclusion of one boundary network) via k-means clustering of voxel-level functional connectivity (FC), constructed structural connectivity (SC) using multi-shell multi-tissue constrained spherical deconvolution with anatomically constrained tractography, and quantified the correlation between SC and FC across within- and between-network edges. Within-network coupling was two to three times higher than between-network coupling in both sessions (Session 1: r within = 0.59 vs. r between = 0.20; Session 2: r within = 0.66 vs. r between = 0.28; p < 0.001). The increased coupling was also observed across subjects, in terms of survived matching of edge counts, and disappeared when network labels were permuted. Network-level coupling was heterogeneous and concentrated in projection pathways spanning the midbrain and medulla oblongata, with rank ordering of the six highest-coupling networks identical across sessions. These findings provide structural support that WMFNs are coherent anatomical-functional units and support reconceptualising WM as a structured contributor to the brain's functional architecture rather than a passive transmission medium.

item.title: Beyond the Group Average: Interindividual Variability in Neural Activity During Written Word Processing
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The processing of language and reading has been a subject of interest for neuropsychologists for many decades. Nevertheless, variability between subjects within the language network has received comparatively little attention. In this study, we employed a precision fMRI approach to examine between-subject variability in neural activity during single-word reading. In order to assess the similarity between subjects' activation patterns, two methods were utilised: Spearman's rank correlation and the Jaccard index. Following this, an exploratory correlation was performed between the similarity and subjects' characteristics. As part of the quantification of between-subject variance, the brain regions characterised by the most variance were identified using interclass correlation coefficients (ICC). The participants exhibited a moderate similarity in their activation patterns, which was correlated with their reading performance and psychopathological traits. Brain regions exhibiting notably high interindividual variability were predominantly located within or adjacent to the language network, suggesting variability in the precise location and extent of the language network among subjects. A comparison of the group-level activation map derived from the same sample revealed that it provided only a moderate representation of the individual maps. The findings underscore the significance of integrating group-level analyses with individual-centred methodologies to achieve more precise characterisation of the neural organisation of language and advance our understanding of the brain-behaviour relation.

item.title: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke's area.
item.description:
Science (New York, N.Y.)
Wernicke's area in the posterior temporal lobe is classically defined by its role in speech comprehension, yet a paradox remains: Why does damage here also profoundly impair speech production? Using direct human brain recordings, cortical stimulation, and lesion analysis, we found that this region is not solely for perception. A discrete subzone within Wernicke's area, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), becomes active before speech, is causally necessary for speech production, and codes features of whole upcoming words rather than low-level acoustics or articulatory information. Its neural activity is distinct from the auditory-feedback responses nearby and can decode intended speech in people with paralysis. Thus, while Wernicke's area is a key part of auditory cortex, it contains a dedicated subregion for speech generation.

item.title: The diastole-systole transition as a regulatory window for heart-brain coupling in major depressive disorder: Evidence from cardiac phase-dependent 1/f slope and periodic neural dynamics.
item.description:
Psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
BACKGROUND: Cardiac rhythms dynamically modulate neural activity and information processing. Disruptions in heart-brain coupling (HBC) may contribute to affective dysregulation in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet their effects on periodic and aperiodic neural activity remain unclear. This study investigated cardiac cycle-dependent modulation of oscillatory and 1/f neural components in MDD. METHODS: Resting-state magnetoencephalography (MEG) and electrocardiography (ECG) were simultaneously recorded from 60 patients with MDD and 60 matched healthy controls. Patients underwent a 6-month follow-up, and remission status was assessed using the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17). The Spectral Parameterization Resolved in Time (SPRiNT) algorithm was used to separate periodic and aperiodic neural activity. Linear mixed-effects models and permutation-based statistics were applied to examine cardiac phase-dependent neural modulation and between-group differences. RESULTS: Cardiac phase modulated both oscillatory power and aperiodic 1/f dynamics. Compared with controls, patients with MDD exhibited attenuated steepening of the aperiodic 1/f spectrum in the left insula during the diastole-to-systole transition and a greater reduction in δ-band power in the left anterior cingulate cortex during late systole. In addition, patients with MDD showed earlier α-band peak activity in the posterior cingulate cortex. Exploratory longitudinal analyses showed an increase in left insular 1/f modulation within remitters, although the formal group × time interaction was not significant. CONCLUSIONS: MDD is characterized by disrupted cardiac cycle-dependent neural dynamics involving both periodic and aperiodic activity. Altered insular aperiodic modulation may reflect impaired excitation-inhibition balance and abnormal heart-brain synchronization in depression, highlighting cardiac rhythms as potential state-dependent targets for closed-loop neuromodulation.

item.title: Deep Clustering of fMRI with Global-Local Feature Extraction for Functional Brain Activity Analysis.
item.description:
IEEE transactions on bio-medical engineering
Clustering is essential for identifying patterns in data. In neuroscience, it is widely used on functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data to uncover brain activity patterns during cognitive tasks and rest. However, traditional methods like K-means struggle with the high dimensionality and temporal complexity of fMRI data, and often fail to capture spatial or contextual structures in image data, limiting their effectiveness. To address these challenges, we propose a deep clustering model that leverages the complementary strengths of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and Masked Autoencoder (MAE) for comprehensive feature extraction. The SAE captures global features and reduces data dimensionality while preserving overall structure. In parallel, the MAE reconstructs masked input patches to learn local contextual features-temporal for sequential data like fMRI, and spatial for imagedata. The combination of global and local features yields a more informative representation of the data. These fused features are then fed into a Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC) module, which iteratively refines cluster centers and feature representations using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss, improving clustering accuracy and robust ness. Experimental results show that our model effectively identifies functional brain activity patterns in task based fMRI and differentiates hippocampal subregions in resting-state fMRI. Overall, our approach offers a unified and versatile deep clustering framework capable of handling various data modalities, enabling more accurate and interpretable analysis in both neuroimaging and general high-dimensional data applications. The proposed framework explicitly decomposes global and local feature learning, overcoming limitations of single path deep clustering methods and providing physiologically meaningful clustering patterns.

item.title: Quantity and quality of children's screen use and their neural and associated behavioral outcomes: A systematic review.
item.description:
Child development
The developmental impact of screen use on young children remains an active area of inquiry, with evidence of both risks and benefits depending on quantity and quality of exposure. This systematic review synthesized 23 neuroimaging studies of children aged 0-8 years, selected from 19,699 records identified across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and APA PsycINFO (2012-2025). Studies were included if they examined typically developing children, employed neuroimaging methods (EEG, fNIRS, or MRI), and assessed the effects of digital media exposure or intervention on brain and associated outcomes. Eight studies on quantity associated greater screen exposure with lower prefrontal activation, altered cortical activity, differences in white matter pathways, and lower myelination in language and cognitive regions. Fifteen studies on quality found that interactive and multimodal media, educational gamification, and caregiver co-use enhanced networks supporting language, perception, and socioemotional skills, whereas non-educational media showed null effects. Our paper argues that discussions on screen use should move beyond the sole focus on duration of screen-time to consider the dimensions of design, content, and context of media use and how they may shape developmental outcomes.

item.title: Causal dynamic resonance reduces false positives in detecting causality.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Many dynamical systems in nature, such as brains and weather systems, are highly nonlinear and complex. Determining information flow among the components that make up these dynamical systems is challenging. If the components are the result of a common process or become synchronized, causality measures typically fail. We previously introduced Cross-Dynamical Delay Differential Analysis, a nonlinear method for assessing causal influence, along with a complementary approach for dynamical similarity between time series data, Dynamical Ergodicity Delay Differential Analysis. Here, we show that "Causal Dynamic Resonance (CDR)" further improves the false positive rejection rate by adding white noise to the data, without perturbing the underlying dynamical system. This is followed by a study of CDR in coupled Rössler systems, where ground truth interactions are known and in invasive intracranial electroencephalographic data from drug-resistant epilepsy patients undergoing presurgical monitoring.

item.title: A "Basin of Attraction" Theory of Speech Initiation and Stuttering.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Recent work in motor neuroscience suggests that well-learned actions are implemented as stable, stereotyped trajectories in neural state space. The purpose of this article was to propose a theory of the neural basis of speech initiation that extends this idea to speech production and identifies a specific disruption that may underlie speech dysfluencies in stuttering. We advance a conceptual framework in which the motor program for a familiar word corresponds to a stable neural trajectory with an associated basin of attraction. We integrate findings from primate motor control, human speech neuroscience, and basal ganglia physiology to specify the role of the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical (BGTC) circuit in initiating these trajectories. We propose that fluent speech depends on the ability of the BGTC circuit to steer the distributed speech motor network into the basin of attraction of the upcoming word's motor program. Stuttering arises when this process is unreliable or poorly coordinated, preventing the motor program from being executed until the neural state is corrected or the effective basin of attraction is broadened through compensatory mechanisms. The basin of attraction framework provides a mechanistic description of the proximal neural processes responsible for stuttering events that can account for a wide range of behavioral and neurophysiological findings in stuttering. It also aligns stuttering theory with contemporary dynamical systems approaches to motor control and generates testable predictions for future neurophysiological and neuroimaging studies.

item.title: Differential Impacts of Acoustic Challenge on Three Language-Related Event-Related Brain Potential Components During Speech Processing: Evidence From the N400, the P600, and a Late Frontal Response.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
When listening to acoustically challenging speech, listeners may strategically shift neural resources across multiple language-related cognitive processes in order to compensate for the additional demands. In the current study, we examined the impact of acoustic challenge (via speech-shaped background noise) on three language-related event-related brain potentials (ERPs): the N400 and two late positivities following the N400-a posterior P600 to syntactic violations and a late frontal effect sensitive to word expectancy. Young, normal-hearing adults (N = 48) listened in quiet and in noise (+3 dB SNR speech-shaped stationary noise) to contextually constraining sentences that ended in an expected word, an unexpected word, or a morphosyntactic violation of the expected word, while electroencephalography data were collected. Replicating prior work, we showed that an N400 expectancy effect was both reduced in amplitude and delayed in onset latency in noise. Providing novel insights into late ERP components, we found that a P600 syntax effect was reduced in amplitude by the presence of background noise. We additionally observed that the P600 response was only present for trials in which the listener successfully identified syntactic violations (irrespective of noise). In contrast to the reductions in the N400 and P600, the late frontal response was not reduced in noise. Collectively, this suggests that, while semantic retrieval and syntactic integration may be impaired by acoustic challenge, young, normal-hearing listeners may still prioritize neural resources toward prediction-related processes to help compensate for increased perceptual demands.

item.title: Shared and distinct neural pathways of aversive and appetitive pain-related learning.
item.description:
Communications biology
Aversive and appetitive learning are central to adaptive behaviour, and pain and avoidance are powerful examples of such forces shaping human behaviour. Alterations in learning are thought to contribute to the development and maintenance of chronic pain, yet their neural underpinnings remain unclear. In this registered within-subject fMRI study (German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS-ID: DRKS00027448), we examined both aversive and appetitive pain learning during acquisition and extinction in 68 healthy individuals. Ratings confirm successful learning, with exploratory analyses suggesting stronger aversive acquisition and incomplete extinction. Both conditions engage the visual cortex during acquisition, with increased connectivity to the right operculum. Aversive acquisition further elicits stronger mediodorsal thalamus activity and heightened connectivity with the locus coeruleus, alongside sustained parahippocampal activation during extinction. Incomplete aversive extinction is linked to ongoing visual cortex activity during pain anticipation. Findings suggest shared neural substrates, but stronger aversive recruitment of rapid encoding and persistent memory systems.

item.title: Brain extracellular matrix remodelling in health and neuropsychiatric disorders.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
The neural extracellular matrix (ECM) is increasingly recognized as an active regulator of brain function and an important contributor to the pathogenesis of neuropsychiatric disorders. This Review examines ECM organization, function and adaptive remodelling in the healthy brain and synthesizes evidence for its pathophysiological alterations in schizophrenia, major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder. Based on findings from human studies and animal models, we propose an ECM-extended conceptual framework of major psychiatric diseases in which polygenic liability, stress exposure and neuroinflammatory signalling converge to remodel the ECM in circuits supporting reward processing, emotion regulation, cognitive control and social cognition. In this model, an early phase of protease-dominant ECM loosening destabilizes microcircuits composed of parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons and principal cells whereas later reactive ECM rebuilding stabilizes dysfunctional network states and contributes to disease persistence, relapse and treatment resistance. This framework positions the ECM as a central hub of genetic, glial, synaptic and systems-level pathogenesis and suggests avenues for the development of ECM-sensitive biomarkers and ECM-directed interventions that may improve the treatment of these disorders.

item.title: Right-to-left shunt burden and altered white matter functional networks in stroke-free patients with patent foramen ovale.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) is a useful technique for investigating the functional organization of human brain networks. Nevertheless, most rsfMRI studies in patent foramen ovale (PFO) have focused on gray-matter connectivity or structural imaging, whereas white-matter functional networks remain poorly characterized. PFO has been hypothesized to expose the brain to recurrent right-to-left shunt (RLS)-related microembolic, vasoactive and hemodynamic stressors, but whether these stressors are associated with altered white-matter functional organization in patients without overt stroke is unclear. The current study used rsfMRI to evaluate white-matter functional networks in stroke-free PFO patients and healthy controls. In the PFO group, RLS severity and anatomical features were characterized using contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler and transesophageal echocardiography. Nine large-scale white-matter networks were identified by K-means clustering of voxel-wise white-matter functional connectivity. Evaluation of spontaneous oscillations and inter-network functional connectivity showed that PFO patients had widespread reductions in fast Fourier transform-derived band-averaged amplitude, mainly involving motor, occipital, cerebellar, deep and cingulum networks, and consistently reduced inferior frontal-to-fronto-temporal connectivity across frequency bands. Higher RLS grade was associated with lower white-matter amplitude in several networks, whereas PFO anatomical measurements showed no independent associations after multiple-comparison correction. Exploratory mediation analyses showed no significant indirect pathways after FDR correction. In this cross-sectional study, these findings suggest that RLS burden may be relevant to subclinical white-matter functional vulnerability in stroke-free PFO.

item.title: Mismatch Negativity and General Cognitive Ability - A Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Intelligence or general cognitive ability (GCA) is fundamental to human behavior and cognition. It impacts important life outcomes like educational success, and even health and longevity have been related to differences in GCA. Understanding the biological basis of such individual variations presents a crucial goal of neuroscience. The mismatch negativity (MMN) is an event-related brain potential that can be measured when-within a series of frequent standard stimuli, rare deviants are presented-and is suggested to reflect conscious (active) or unconscious (passive) detection processes of the brain. Importantly, variations in MMN amplitude and latency have been linked to differences in GCA. Yet findings vary considerably. This preregistered meta-analysis provides a comprehensive and structured overview of the current state of research. Following the study selection process in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, and the rating of study design quality with the Study Design and Implementation Assessment Device for Individual Difference Research (DIAD-ID), the association between GCA and MMN amplitude and latency was examined in 645 healthy adults across 12 included studies. The estimated across-sample associations between MMN and GCA were small, but significant (MMN amplitude-GCA: r = -0.09, MMN latency-GCA: r = -0.16; p < 0.01) and moderators were identified. Between-sample heterogeneity was moderate, with no evidence of publication bias. Our findings suggest that higher cognitive ability is associated with slightly stronger and faster MMN responses. However, the low estimated across-sample effect sizes and the small number of included studies also highlight the need for more research.

item.title: Where could the brain keep a symbol?
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Neuroscience routinely describes memories as stored neural symbols, yet durable memory and successful retrieval do not establish a separately accessible symbolic vehicle. I distinguish retention, the claim that a physical change persists and later influences behavior, from symbolic storage, the stronger computational claim that a description can be accessed independently of the operation it specifies. The criterion is functional and system-relative and does not rule out neural activity as access. It requires specifying, before testing, the candidate vehicle, its proposed use, the system boundary, and an endogenous route reaching the vehicle without using it. DNA meets the criterion: replication preserves nucleotide sequence without producing the encoded gene product. Evidence from synapses and circuits establishes persistent, functionally useful organization but has not shown this separation for any neural memory vehicle; in these states, identified reads are executions that modify what they read. Hippocampal replay, neuromodulation, and artificial-network checkpoints show that the verdict depends on the vehicle and operations compared. I agree with Gallistel that intracellular nucleic acid mechanisms could provide a genuine store, but disagree that behavioral precision alone requires one. Maintained coupling, in which memory is sustained by continual recalibration rather than read from a store, offers an alternative whose predictions depend on error source: drift can be corrected where a reference signal remains, but a unique, never-revisited episode offers none. Current evidence favors retention without symbolic storage in synapses and circuits; I propose operational tests that could overturn this verdict. Either way, retention and use remain memory.

item.title: Microstructural disruption of the forceps minor in schizophrenia: a potential clinical imaging biomarker using translational DTI.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Schizophrenia is one of the most complex brain disorders, arising from multidimensional pathophysiological processes that span genetic vulnerability, neurotransmitter dysregulation, structural brain damage, and large-scale brain network dysfunction. Large-scale neuroimaging studies have consistently demonstrated the critical role of frontal brain regions in schizophrenia. Despite substantial progress, the precise localization of structural damage within these regions and the neurobiological mechanisms linking such alterations to disease pathology remain poorly understood. In this study, we included a total of 115 subjects from two sites of the B-SNIP dataset, comprising 60 healthy controls and 55 individuals with schizophrenia. We employed diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to precisely characterize specific structural alterations in the frontal brain regions associated with schizophrenia. Our findings reveal significant microstructural abnormalities in the forceps minor, a major commissural white-matter tract that serves as a critical interhemispheric bridge between the bilateral frontal lobes. Network-level mapping further demonstrates that the forceps minor is closely integrated with large-scale brain networks, particularly the default mode network, and maintains strong structural connectivity with orbitofrontal regions-both of which are known to exhibit dysfunction in schizophrenia. Moreover, converging evidence suggests that the forceps minor plays an important role in the regulation of social behavior, a core domain of impairment in schizophrenia. Collectively, these findings identify the forceps minor as a promising structural imaging biomarker for schizophrenia and provide novel insights into the microstructural mechanisms underlying the disorder.

item.title: Cortical Hypoperfusion in Acute Anorexia Nervosa Is Graded Along the Sensorimotor-Association Hierarchy.
item.description:
The International journal of eating disorders
Cortical gray-matter changes in anorexia nervosa (AN) are among the largest reported in psychiatry, but the functional-metabolic state of that tissue is largely unknown. Because cortical energy use is highest in transmodal association cortex (prefrontal, parietal, and temporal regions of the default-mode and frontoparietal networks), a reduced energy supply predicts a graded rather than uniform reduction in perfusion (blood delivery to tissue). A total of 44 acutely underweight women with AN and 45 healthy women underwent 3 T pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling with partial-volume correction. Cerebral blood flow was compared between groups across the Schaefer 100 regions 7 networks atlas, age-adjusted and false-discovery-rate-corrected, and the case-control map was compared with the principal functional gradient (the axis running from sensorimotor to transmodal cortex), with cortical thickness in the same participants, and with 18 PET and SPECT receptor maps. Perfusion was lower in AN in 97 of 100 regions and maximal in orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex (composite d = -0.56). The deficit scaled with position along the principal functional gradient (ρ = -0.56), an axis unrelated to perfusion in health, and was recoverable in individual brains (d = -0.53). Thinning was widespread but unrelated to gradient position, and the two effect maps did not correspond. Hypoperfusion was greater where D1, CB1, mGluR5, M1, 5-HT2A, and μ-opioid systems are dense, the dopaminergic, cannabinoid, glutamatergic, and muscarinic ones persisting after gradient adjustment. Cortical perfusion in acute AN is not uniformly reduced but organized along the cortex's principal functional axis, dissociable from cortical thinning and aligned with reward-related neurochemistry.

item.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels.
item.description:
eLife
Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse's contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

item.title: Timing and meaning in spoken thought relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
When people think aloud, their reports vary in duration and in how closely successive thoughts are related in meaning. We asked whether these two dimensions relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics. Using 10-minute think-aloud fMRI scans from 75 adults, we quantified timing as variability in sentence-event duration and semantic continuity as similarity between adjacent grouped thoughts. In models including both measures, greater duration variability was associated with lower relative brain entropy (BEN), estimated from BOLD time series, in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (voxel wise FDR q < 0.05). This association persisted after adjustment for speech coverage, pause duration, articulation rate and event count. Semantic continuity was associated with differences in BOLD amplitude and synchrony across bilateral sensorimotor regions. These voxel wise associations fell below the FDR threshold after adjustment for speech coverage or pause duration. In a secondary atlas-based analysis, semantic continuity remained positively associated with local synchrony in Default C after adjustment for speech timing (β = 0.517, P = 0.003). These findings link the timing of spoken reports to dorsolateral prefrontal brain activity irregularity and show how the sensorimotor correlates of semantic continuity covary with speech timing.

item.title: Distinct developmental organization of intrinsic brain dynamics supports different components of inhibitory control during adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescent inhibitory control develops within a changing organization of intrinsic brain activity, yet the signal properties and cortical systems associated with different control demands remain unclear. We studied 101 youths aged 8-18 years using brain entropy (BEN), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Voxelwise and seven-network models evaluated age associations and task-by-age interactions while adjusting for sex, head motion, and gray-matter anatomy. Spatially standardized ALFF showed age associations in somatomotor and salience/ventral-attention networks. Contextual control, assessed with the AX Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), showed the broadest age-dependent coupling: all four spatially standardized measures yielded voxelwise interactions surviving permutation-based cluster false discovery rate correction, and the frontoparietal BEN interaction survived network correction. Better action cancellation was associated with higher frontoparietal BEN without a corrected network age interaction. Independent cortical references further differentiated these patterns: raw BEN age-effect evidence was stronger toward association cortex, whereas the ALFF-AX-CPT age interaction was stronger toward sensorimotor cortex. Additional task interactions aligned with the second and third connectivity gradients. Core voxelwise AX-CPT findings persisted after age trimming. These findings link the differentiation of inhibitory-control demands to the developmental organization of complementary intrinsic signal properties across cortical systems, highlighting contextual control as a prominent locus of age-dependent brain-behavior coupling.

item.title: Beyond morphometry: Adolescent brain microarchitecture reflects sex differences in pubertal timing and hormones
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Puberty is a sensitive neurodevelopmental period characterized by dramatic increases in adrenal and gonadal hormones, yet how these changes relate to human brain microarchitecture remains unclear. Here, we used restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) to link peripubertal hormone levels to individual differences in brain microarchitecture (i.e., cellular and neurite density) in 7,457 youth (ages 9 to 13 years) from the ABCD Study. Sex- and age-stratified multi-task regression analyses identified microarchitecture patterns jointly associated with physical pubertal maturation and each dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), testosterone, estradiol (in female youth), in turn, combining repeated cross-validation with permutation-based feature importance. At ages 9 to 11 years, microarchitecture differences explained 11-13% of pubertal hormone variability in female youth and 4-6% in male youth. Further, microarchitecture features were differentially associated with pubertal hormones. Younger male youth exhibited widespread pubertal hormone-related differences in neurite density that consolidated into fewer, stronger associations with age, while female youth exhibited age-related expansion in pubertal cellular density differences. Anatomically, hormone-relevant microarchitecture consistently included reward processing hubs (e.g., pallidum, accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex). Because animal models suggest that DHEA and testosterone metabolites have opposing effects on GABAergic signaling, we hypothesize that future research should investigate gray matter microarchitecture for insight into pubertal hormone contributions to adolescent refinement of excitatory-inhibitory balance. Ultimately, these findings provide a starting point for investigating how pubertal endocrine changes shape reward circuitry and neurotransmitter systems, with potential implications for the pubertal emergence of sex differences in adolescent psychopathology.

item.title: Neural processing of linguistic speech features and their modulation by selective attention in users of hearing aids and cochlear implants
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding speech relies on the neural processing of acoustic and linguistic features, which can both be analyzed using Temporal Response Functions (TRFs). While both types of features have been the focus of numerous studies in typical-hearing individuals, much less is known about the neural processing of continuous speech for people with hearing loss, particularly how hearing-impaired listeners process word-level features in noisy environments, where they typically struggle. We recorded EEG from hearing aid (HA, n=29) and cochlear implant (CI, n=24) users, and an age-matched typical-hearing (TH) control group (n=29), while participants listened to audiobook segments in quiet and with a competing speaker, using their personal hearing devices (CI and HA). A hierarchical encoding framework incrementally added word onset, word frequency, and word surprisal as predictors of the EEG signal. Attentional modulation was assessed by comparing encoding scores for attended versus ignored speech. All three groups showed clear neural responses to word onset, frequency, and surprisal for speech in quiet. Surprisal tracking emerged at 400~ms in TH participants, 500~ms in HA users, and 600~ms in CI users, weakest in the CI group. All three groups exhibited attentional modulation of surprisal tracking. Word frequency yielded significant encoding gains in quiet only for TH and HI listeners, not CI users. We show for the first time that CI users exhibit significant, attention-modulated neural responses to word surprisal. More broadly, surprisal tracking was present across all hearing-impaired groups but weakest in CI users, the cohort with the greatest difficulty understanding speech in noise.

item.title: Neural sensitivity to musical rhythm is associated with the temporal dynamics of statistical learning in speech
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Statistical learning enables the extraction of structure from the environment, including word units from continuous speech. Yet inter-individual variability suggests contributions from other, potentially broader domain-general mechanisms. Here, we investigated whether individual differences in music rhythm processing are associated with the dynamics of statistical learning during speech segmentation, potentially reflecting shared sensitivity to temporal regularities across music and language. Adults were exposed to structured and random artificial speech streams while neural tracking at syllable and word rate frequencies was tracked over time using EEG to characterize the emergence of word representations. In addition, participants’ abilities to process rhythm in musical materials were assessed using behavioral and neural (EEG) measures. Neural measurements revealed robust tracking at the syllabic level in both structured and random streams, whereas word-level tracking emerged over exposure only in the structured stream condition. Importantly, individual differences in neural synchronization to musical rhythms were associated with the temporal dynamics of word extraction. These results suggest that individual differences in the ability to process temporal regularities in musical material are related to the efficiency with which statistical regularities are extracted from sequential language material. More broadly, the findings provide evidence for domain-general mechanisms supporting sensitivity to temporal structure regularities across auditory domains.

item.title: Neural correlates of individual differences in cognition: a behavioral performance, EEG, and MRI dataset
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The Mainz Network Study provides comprehensive behavioral and multimodal neural data from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years from the general population, supporting research on interindividual differences in cognitive ability. The multi-indicator design supports latent-variable modeling of all major constructs alongside their structural, functional, and electrophysiological neural correlates. Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time). Electroencephalography (EEG) data was collected during four resting-state blocks and during task performance (cognitive control and processing speed). High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging using the SANDI protocol, and multi-band multi-echo functional MRI during rest and task-switching were acquired in a subset. Behavioral, EEG, and MRI data are accessible via a RDC-ZPID repository. All data are BIDS-organized and shared raw.
