item.title: Reconsidering the Psychotomimetic Properties of LSD: Connectome-Based Classification Reveals Partial Overlap with First Episode Psychosis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The acute effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) have long been compared to early psychosis. Despite this, no studies have compared the acute effects of LSD and psychosis on resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) with parallel approaches. We used connectome-based classification, a data-driven method, to distinguish between medication-naïve, non-affective first episode psychosis (FEP) and the acute effects of LSD. Separate classifiers were trained to distinguish the acute effects of LSD from placebo and FEP patients from matched healthy controls. The LSD-placebo classifier was then validated on an external LSD-placebo dataset. The network-interaction classifiers with good discriminability were then applied across datasets to evaluate whether LSD-related connectivity patterns could classify FEP as being LSD-like and vice versa. Subsequently, we investigated univariate RSFC between select networks, based on which network-interactions the classifiers suggested might overlap in LSD and FEP. Cross-application of externally validated LSD-placebo classifiers revealed partial overlap between LSD and FEP, particularly involving the dorsal attention network (DAN) and sensorimotor network (SMN). Application of the most discriminant FEP-HC network-interaction classifiers revealed that LSD displayed select similarities with FEP. Univariate network analysis also supports between-network DAN and SMN dysconnectivity being a point of convergence. Our findings indicate that neural correlates of FEP might have select overlaps with changes in brain functioning produced by LSD. These results suggest serotonergic dysfunction might play a role in the early stages of psychosis and necessitate future studies directly comparing FEP and LSD.

item.title: Spatial trapping and anteroposterior segregation of the default mode network in schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The spatial organisation of the default mode network (DMN) across recurrent brain configurations remains poorly understood in schizophrenia. Here, we introduce two indices to quantify how selectively a network is represented across brain modes and whether selected anterior and posterior regions participate in the same configurations. Resting-state functional MRI from 16 healthy controls and 11 participants with non-acute schizophrenia was used to assess static and dynamic functional connectivity, global synchronisation, intrinsic ignition and variability measures. Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis identified the brain modes. The Spatial Trapping Index (STI) measured the distribution of relative network composition across four modes, while anterior–posterior co-participation (CAP) measured shared these modes. The two indices were compared using permutation test within Holm correction. Static functional connectivity was lower within the dorsal attention network, while dynamic functional connectivity showed greater variability in several network. No significant differences were detected in global synchronisation, intrinsic ignition or the three signatures of metastability. Mean DMN composition was similar between groups, but STI was higher in SCZ, while CAP was lower. Bootstrap resampling retained the observed directions in 89.6% of STI contrasts and 91.9% of CAP contrasts. These findings suggest that DMN representation is less selective across brain modes in schizophrenia, while selected anterior and posterior regions participate less consistently together. STI and CAP offer a new way to quantify these complementary aspects of spatial organisation, providing a basis for investigating their clinical relevance.

item.title: Saccadic network dysfunction underlies eye-movement variability in early Parkinson's disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Parkinson’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by altered subcortical-cortical connectivity, leading to motor and cognitive deficits. Saccadic eye movement abnormalities are among the earliest and most persistent markers of the disease, serving as sensitive indicators of disrupted oculomotor and cognitive control. While changes in average saccadic behavioral measures are widely reported in Parkinson's disease, intra-individual variability in saccadic performance and the underlying network dysfunction remain poorly understood. Here, we quantified intra-individual saccadic variability in early-stage Parkinson’s disease and identified its functional correlates within the resting-state saccadic network. We analyzed data from the inclusion visit of 91 patients with early-stage Parkinson’s disease and 46 healthy controls from the ICEBERG cohort (monocentric prospective research study) who underwent oculomotor testing and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. First, at the behavioral level, we assessed intra-individual variability in saccadic performance within each group using the coefficient of variation of reaction time and normalized peak velocity across trials. Second, at the brain level, we assessed group differences in static and dynamic functional connectivity across 39 regions comprising the saccadic network. We examined the relationship between network connectivity and saccadic variability using partial least squares analysis. We also quantified network organization using graph-theory measures of global efficiency and clustering coefficient. Finally, we tested the relevance of intra-individual saccadic variability and network features in distinguishing patients from healthy controls using a multivariate Mahalanobis classifier. Our results showed that, compared to HC, patients had higher intra-individual variability in saccadic behavioral measures of reaction time (p Holm = 0.012) and normalized peak velocity (p Holm = 0.012). Interestingly, patients had (i) reduced static and dynamic connectivity within the saccadic network and (ii) weaker associations between network connectivity and intra-individual saccadic variability of specifically normalized peak velocity. These results were particularly driven by regions within the cognitive saccade network. The classifier that integrated intra-individual saccadic variability and network connectivity achieved 95.62% accuracy in distinguishing patients from healthy controls, with dynamic connectivity contributing more strongly to classification performance than static connectivity. We demonstrate that elevated intra-individual variability of saccades, underpinned by altered functional connectivity within cognitive-oculomotor networks, is a prominent feature of early-stage Parkinson’s disease. Emerging as a promising physiological marker of disease pathophysiology, intra-individual variability offers a powerful new framework to refine early diagnosis and improve the tracking of neurodegeneration before severe clinical milestones are reached.

item.title: Aperiodic EEG Activity Is a Domain-Specific Marker of Attentional Aging in Neurotypical Adults.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Aperiodic neural activity has been reliably shown to be reduced among older adults, and these reductions are associated with age-related cognitive decline. These results suggest that aperiodic activity, as measured by the spectral exponent, might be a viable electrophysiological biomarker for cognitive aging. However, this has not been tested longitudinally, within participants, during normal aging. Here, we used a longitudinal cohort of either sex to test whether changes in aperiodic activity between two sessions, ∼5 years apart, track behavioral change across two domains: sustained attention (Psychomotor Vigilance Test) and executive function (modified Simon task). We found that aperiodic activity declined within individuals after the interval, independent of age at baseline. This within-person change tracked concurrent changes in reaction times during sustained attention but was not associated with changes in any Simon task measure. Within a resampling framework, the aperiodic-PVT association was stable across cohort resamples and independently fitted partitions, though it was not confirmed in a small, frozen held-out set. These findings suggest the longitudinal decline in aperiodic activity tracks attentional processing speed rather than executive function, supporting its potential as a domain-specific biomarker of attentional aging in neurotypical populations.

item.title: Probing the Neural Geometry of Conscious Object Perception in Time.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a "coarse-to-fine" sequence or a "fine-to-coarse" sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. In contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level.

item.title: Perception of Tones versus Tone Streams under Random Multi-tone Masking and Its Representation in Auditory Cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream.

item.title: Representation of Emotional Expressions across the Face and Voice Brain Networks.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is fundamental to successful social interaction, yet how the brain represents emotional information across sensory systems remains unclear. Here, we systematically mapped the contribution of individually defined face- and voice-selective cortical regions in 24 human participants of either sex to unimodal and crossmodal emotion expressions. Using multivariate pattern classification, we show that emotional expressions are robustly decodable from the dominant sensory modality across all individually defined face- and voice-selective areas and that these representations cannot be accounted for by low- and mid-level stimulus properties alone. Strikingly, emotional information from the nondominant modality-vocal expressions within face networks and facial expressions within voice networks-was also represented throughout the network, with the exception of the occipital face areas. Crossmodal decoding further revealed a shared neural code for facial and vocal emotions in the temporal voice areas, posterior superior temporal sulcus, and precentral gyrus, indicating that these regions contain emotion representations that generalize across sensory modalities. Furthermore, in most face- and voice-selective regions, audiovisual emotional expressions could be distinguished from representations elicited by the dominant unimodal modality, indicating that bimodal signals are not simply represented as their strongest sensory component. Together, these findings reveal that emotion representations are distributed broadly across face- and voice-selective regions and identify temporofrontal regions as key sites supporting modality-independent emotion representations.

item.title: Robust sex differences in regional gray matter volume but shared personality-gray matter associations in young adults.
item.description:
PloS one
Relationships between personality traits and brain regions have been widely studied, but potential sex-based differences have received less attention, despite sex hormones affecting neuronal activity and brain functions. We aimed to determine whether the personality-brain relationship differs fundamentally between the sexes. We enrolled healthy university students (103 men, 111 women). Gray matter volumes were measured in 388 brain regions using voxel-based morphometry on T1-weighted brain MRI, and personality traits were assessed using the temperament and character inventory. In confirmatory analyses correcting for multiple comparisons across all 388 regions and seven factors (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate), main-effect sex differences in gray matter volume were robust: 17 regions survived correction, independent of personality, and were predominantly subcortical (thalamus, pallidum and putamen) and right-lateralized. By contrast, neither any association between personality and gray matter volume nor any personality-by-sex interaction survived correction, indicating that personality-gray matter associations were not detectably different between the sexes. In a cross-validated penalized regression over all regions, only self-transcendence was predicted above chance (out-of-sample R2 ≈ 0.04, permutation p = 0.004), and this prediction was essentially unchanged after adjustment for sex and total intracranial volume. In exploratory region-wise analyses (uncorrected p < 0.05), the distribution of brain regions associated with each personality factor appeared to differ between the sexes; for instance, harm avoidance in females was related mainly to parietal, temporal and thalamic regions, whereas in males it was related mainly to sensorimotor and cerebellar regions. These exploratory patterns did not survive correction and are reported as hypothesis-generating observations. Overall, sex differences in this young adult sample were robust for subcortical volume but not for the coupling between personality and gray matter volume, which appeared largely shared between the sexes, underscoring the importance of considering sex as a biological variable while distinguishing confirmed effects from exploratory observations.

item.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Functions in Patients With Essential Tremor Without Dementia: Beyond the Cerebellum.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Essential tremor (ET) is characterized not only by motor disturbances but also, in many cases, by a wide array of cognitive symptoms. Accumulating evidence implicates pathways beyond the cerebellum by which cognitive changes emerge. However, the extracerebellar neuropathologic correlates of specific cognitive symptoms have not been examined. This study evaluated these potential clinicopathologic associations in older adults with ET. Methods Participants were adults ≥55 years with ET who were followed prospectively and longitudinally and donated their brains for neuropathologic evaluation as part of the Clinical-Pathological Study of Cognitive Impairment in Essential Tremor study. Cognitive outcomes included attention, executive function, language, memory, and visuospatial function. Postmortem neuropathologic assessment included Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) neuritic plaque scores, Thal β-amyloid A score, Braak and Braak neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) stage, and Braak Lewy pathology stage. Regional cerebral cortical atrophy ratings (neocortical and hippocampal), cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and markers of cerebrovascular health were also rated. Regression models examined neuropathologic correlates of cognitive function, adjusting for numerous confounders. Sensitivity analyses examined robustness of findings. Results The sample consisted of 57 individuals with ET and without dementia (mean age = 88.6 ± 5.4 years; 54.4% female, 71.9% cognitively normal, 28.1% with mild cognitive impairment). Higher amyloid burden was associated with lower attention (CERAD β = -0.48, p < 0.001; Thal β = -0.37, p < 0.01) and lower executive function (CERAD β = -0.40, p 0.01; Thal β = -0.33, p = 0.01). CERAD score was associated with lower language (β = -0.31, p = 0.04). Braak NFT stage was associated with lower attention (β = -0.26, p = 0.04) and lower executive function (β = -0.28, p = 0.03). Hippocampal atrophy was associated with lower memory performance (β = -0.29, p = 0.04). Discussion Core pathologies of AD, amyloid and tau, are associated with decrements in attention and executive function in older adults with ET and without dementia, while hippocampal atrophy is associated with lower memory performance. These results, consistent with a growing literature on extracerebellar pathologies in ET, suggest that multidomain cognitive symptoms among older adults with ET and without dementia may be driven in large part by AD-related cortical degenerative processes. Ongoing work is examining the molecular basis of these processes. Limitations include a highly educated, demographically homogeneous, and relatively small sample, as well as a lack of a control group.

item.title: Distinct Amygdala-Frontopolar and Amygdala-Medial Temporal Pathways Support Temporal Memory for Emotional Events.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Growing evidence suggests that emotion shapes temporal aspects of memory-such as remembering when an event occurred-yet the neural bases of these effects remain unclear. Prior work indicates that temporal context representations in memory are supported by the functions of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and prefrontal regions, including hippocampus, perirhinal cortex, and lateral frontopolar cortex (FPl). These regions have privileged access to amygdala-originated affective signals that may mediate emotional influences on temporal memory. To test whether these candidate pathways shape temporal memory for emotional events, participants encoded trial-unique negative and positive images in the scanner, followed by a surprise temporal memory task. We found that more negative stimuli were associated with greater amygdala activation and lower temporal memory error for when emotional images occurred. Replicating and extending prior work, higher stimulus-evoked multivoxel pattern similarity in the hippocampus and FPl was associated with higher temporal memory error. Notably, greater amygdala responding to emotional images predicted higher between-trial pattern similarity in the hippocampus but lower within- and between-trial similarity in FPl. Amygdala engagement was also correlated with greater perirhinal activation, which in turn predicted stronger item memory and a recency bias in temporal memory estimates. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct-and opposing-modulatory effects of amygdala-FPl and amygdala-MTL pathways on temporal memory, with the potential to sharpen and blur memory for when emotional events occurred.

item.title: Early Neural Responses to Negative Emotional Processing and Longitudinal Grief Trajectories in Later Life.
item.description:
Psychotherapy and psychosomatics
Introduction While most bereaved adults adapt to their loss within a year, 3-10% develop Prolonged Grief Disorder. The neurobiological substrates of adaptive versus maladaptive grief trajectories remain poorly understood. Methods In this longitudinal study, ninety-seven adults (50-83 years) bereaved within the past year completed task-based fMRI (an emotional face-matching paradigm) and resting-state fMRI at study baseline. Grief symptoms were repeatedly assessed over 12 months. Voxel-wise linear mixed-effects models with cluster-wise correction (uncorrected p=.005; alpha=.05) examined associations between baseline fMRI responses to negative emotional faces (fearful and angry) versus shapes and 12-month symptom trajectories, adjusting for demographics, time since loss, and depressive symptoms. Results At baseline, left anterior insula activity was positively associated with loneliness (r=.305) and intrusive thoughts (r=.328). Longitudinally, greater baseline activity in bilateral anterior insula and left amygdala was associated with faster improvement in loneliness (z<-3.01). Lower amygdala-orbitofrontal cortex resting-state connectivity was associated with faster loneliness improvement, with stronger effects at higher depressive symptoms and greater perceived social support. Conversely, greater left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activity (z=3.10) and its task-dependent connectivity with lateral occipital cortices (z=3.18) were associated with slower improvement in avoidant coping. Conclusion Greater engagement of salience network circuit components during negative emotional processing was associated with diminishing loneliness, whereas greater recruitment of prefrontal executive control network node was associated with persistent avoidance. These findings suggest distinct neural pathways underlying adaptive versus maladaptive grief responses. Further research to confirm these observations and to develop early risk stratification and mechanism-informed interventions to prevent prolonged grief is needed.

item.title: Cross-domain encoding models reveal shared and domain-specific neural representations across language and mathematics.
item.description:
Science advances
Whether language and mathematics rely on shared or distinct neural representations remains unresolved in cognitive neuroscience. Here, we combined latent features from a large language model with functional magnetic resonance imaging encoding models to test cross-domain generalization in 32 participants performing sentence comprehension and calculation tasks. Cross-domain prediction identified cortical regions showing partially shared representations, most consistently in the left area 55b, while control analyses suggested that these effects could not be fully explained by low-level visual or task-general factors. Domain-specificity contrasts revealed stronger language-related prediction in the left superior temporal sulcus and angular gyrus and math-related prediction in the left precentral sulcus and bilateral intraparietal sulci. Model-weight analyses revealed distinct weight profiles associated with shared and domain-specific prediction patterns. Cross-domain regions also exhibited task-dependent functional coupling with language- and math-related networks. Together, these findings suggest that language and mathematics involve partially shared neural representations alongside domain-specific cortical organization, helping reconcile previous contrasting views on their neural basis.

item.title: Auditory cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulations is sufficient to support perceptual categorization of speech and music.
item.description:
Science advances
Auditory processing is typically described as hierarchical, culminating in neural representation of abstract categories. However, it remains unclear whether category-selective responses in auditory cortex require representational mechanisms beyond the coding of acoustic features or whether the acoustic representations already available in the auditory cortex are sufficient to account for categorization. Here, we test whether cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulation (STM) features is sufficient to support speech-music categorization by combining human intracranial recordings with continuous behavioral judgments of a naturalistic soundtrack in which speech and music occur both separately and simultaneously. We show that temporal and spectral modulation patterns largely characterize speech and music, respectively, and that cortical auditory regions robustly track these features over time, with distinct oscillatory frequency bands preferentially encoding temporal and spectral modulations. Critically, cortical representations of STMs predicted perceptual categorical judgments gathered in an independent sample. Last, speech- and music-related STM representations showed stronger tracking of category-specific acoustical features in left versus right cortical auditory regions, respectively. These findings indicate that the efficient neural coding of acoustical features provides a sufficient basis for the categorical distinction between speech and music and that the temporal and spectral components of this representation are implemented through distinct oscillatory mechanisms.
